Band Neutrophil.text: Band neutrophils are associated with a left shift, which indicates an increase in circulating immature granulocytes, often seen in response to infection, inflammation, or stress [2][4]. On a peripheral blood film, bands are characterized by unsegmented nuclear morphology and may be seen alongside toxic changes such as toxic granulation, vacuolation, and dohle bodies, which are indicative of toxicity and increased neutrophil activity [1][4]. A severe neutrophilia with a left shift, termed leukaemoid reaction, can also be observed in these conditions [2][4].

Basophil.text: Basophils are associated with conditions such as chronic spontaneous urticaria (CIU/CSU), where basopenia may reflect recruitment to skin tissue, and with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), where marked basophilia is a prognostic feature and diagnostic criterion of disease phases [1][8]. On a peripheral blood film, increased basophil counts can be observed in hyperbasophilia (>1.0 × 10^9/L), often with immature cells in CML, and their presence may be linked to reactive or neoplastic processes [2][3][8]. The film may also show evidence of basophil infiltration in tissues, but specific morphological features are not detailed in the sources.

Eosinophil.text: Eosinophils are associated with a broad range of conditions, including reactive (secondary) and primary (clonal or neoplastic) eosinophilias, as well as hypereosinophilic syndromes involving tissue damage [1][2]. On a peripheral blood film, eosinophils may be identified by their characteristic granulated cytoplasm and bi-lobed or multilobed nuclei, with the degree of eosinophilia categorized as mild, moderate, or severe based on absolute counts [6]. The presence of eosinophilia can be linked to conditions such as hypereosinophilic syndrome, myeloid neoplasms, or allergic and parasitic diseases, with eosinophil infiltration or granule protein aggregates indicating tissue involvement [1][7].

Lymphocyte.text: Lymphocytes are associated with reactive processes, such as infections like COVID-19, where atypical or reactive lymphocytes with heterogeneous morphology are observed, and with neoplastic conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia, which often presents with lymphocytosis and smudge cells on a blood smear [2][4]. In COVID-19, abnormal lymphocytes may appear as atypical, reactive, activated, or pleomorphic, although their morphology does not always correlate with disease severity [2][6]. The presence of lymphocytosis, especially when pleomorphic or with atypical features, can suggest reactive or neoplastic lymphoid proliferations, with the latter often showing clonal populations identified through flow cytometry [1][4].

Monocyte.text: Monocytes are associated with inflammatory conditions such as atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, infections, and hematologic disorders like myeloproliferative diseases [2][4][7][8]. On a peripheral blood film, findings may include monocytosis, which is an elevated monocyte count, and morphological abnormalities such as vacuolation or atypical reactive lymphocytes, especially in cases like COVID-19 [4][6]. These features can support the presence of systemic inflammation or immune response.

Segmented Neutrophil.text: Segmented neutrophils are associated with conditions such as sepsis, where morphological abnormalities like toxic granulations, vacuolation, and hypersegmentation (neutrophil hypersegmentation) can be observed on peripheral blood films [3][7]. In severe infections, toxic granulations indicate increased microbicidal activity, while hypersegmentation is linked to megaloblastic anemia. Additionally, a leukaemoid reaction, characterized by severe neutrophilia with left shift, may show toxic granulations in neutrophils [7].

Monocyte|vacuolated.text: Monocytes are associated with inflammatory conditions such as monocytosis in acute and chronic inflammation, including atherosclerosis, and can be elevated in myelodysplastic syndromes and myeloproliferative disorders [5][6]. On peripheral blood films, monocytes typically show variable nuclear shapes, a ground glass blue-gray cytoplasm with fine granules, and may have pseudopods or vacuoles [1]. Cytoplasmic vacuolation in monocytes can be associated with reactive or infectious states, and in COVID-19, a high proportion of vacuolated monocytes has been linked to milder disease and shorter hospital stays [4].

Segmented Neutrophil|vacuolated.text: Segmented neutrophils are associated with conditions such as sepsis, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), and septic shock, where morphological changes like toxic granulation, Dohle bodies, and cytoplasmic vacuolation are observed [1][8]. On peripheral blood films, these cells may display toxic granules, vacuolation, and Dohle bodies, indicating activation and toxic changes often linked to severe infections or inflammatory states [1][8]. Cytoplasmic vacuolation suggests phagocytic activity, autophagocytosis, or cellular response to infection or inflammation, and its presence can be an indicator of neutrophil activation in severe conditions [1][8].
